repos.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
repos.paper_summary: OpenVLHarness is a multimodal tool-use harness for MLLMs, built around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer wraps heterogeneous perception, search, and computation tools behind task-level interfaces and renders their outputs into model-readable observations. Memory registers images, structured data, and web references under handles, and a Python Coding Agent runs generated programs over stored values, so later steps can reuse earlier evidence. The harness is evaluated on 22 benchmarks across four domains with eight backbones. Averaged over the 22 datasets, it raises Qwen3-VL-8B from 34.2 to 45.4 and Qwen3-VL-32B from 38.3 to 50.9, outperforming OctoTools and Visual Sketchpad. With GPT-6 Luna at medium effort, it scores 56.5 against 45.8 for the base model, and it is reported to outperform Codex and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort while using at most 37% of their model-token cost. Qwen3-VL results are means of three seeds; GPT-6 results are single runs, so their variance is unreported in the main table. The paper's benchmark-level gains are uneven, with some datasets, such as V* for Qwen3-VL-8B, showing no gain.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Extra reasoning budget gives diminishing returns, so the paper proposes OpenVLHarness to add multimodal evidence acquisition.

digest_headlines.heading: Harness Design
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVLHarness pairs a capability layer that renders tool outputs with persistent memory of handle-addressed artifacts.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVLHarness raises Qwen3-VL-8B scores on 22 benchmarks, for example from 32.00 to 48.56 on a counting benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior visual tool-use systems use fixed plans or task-specific frameworks, while this paper keeps multimodal artifacts addressable across turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Released harness gives broad gains on 22 benchmarks and can specialize to domains without updating model weights.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix reports tool-call volume, capability distribution, paired accuracy effects, and object-count distributions of benchmarks.

repos.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
repos.paper_summary:
DSPy is a programming model that compiles declarative language model pipelines into self-improving systems by automatically optimizing prompts and demonstrations. It replaces hard-coded prompt strings with parameterized modules, such as `ChainOfThought` or `ReAct`, which are optimized by "teleprompters." These optimizers bootstrap few-shot examples or finetune smaller models to maximize a user-defined metric.

On the GSM8K math word problem dataset, compiled DSPy programs using GPT-3.5 achieved 81.6% test accuracy, outperforming standard few-shot prompting (72.4%) and expert-created demonstrations (72.4%). For llama2-13b-chat, the best configuration reached 46.9% test accuracy, surpassing the zero-shot baseline of 9.4%. On HotPotQA multi-hop question answering, a compiled multi-hop program with GPT-3.5 achieved 45.6% answer exact match, while a finetuned T5-Large model reached 39.3% on the development set. The paper notes that compiling typically takes minutes to tens of minutes. Limitations include reliance on specific metrics for optimization and the fact that results are reported on only two case studies.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hand-written prompt templates for LM pipelines are brittle, and the paper proposes DSPy to replace them with optimizable modules.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing toolkits rely on hand-written prompt templates, while DSPy aims to optimize arbitrary multi-stage LM pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: The DSPy Programming Model
digest_headlines.headline: DSPy programs combine typed signatures, parameterized modules, and teleprompters that optimize all modules against a metric.

digest_headlines.heading: The DSPy Compiler
digest_headlines.headline: The compiler runs three stages: bootstrapping candidate demonstrations, selecting among them, and optimizing control flow.

digest_headlines.heading: Goals of Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation hypothesizes that DSPy can replace hand-written prompts without losing quality, adapt across LMs, and enable richer pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: Case Study: Math Word Problems
digest_headlines.headline: Compiled DSPy programs improve GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat on math word problems from 4–20% accuracy to 49–88%.

digest_headlines.heading: Case Study: Complex Question Answering
digest_headlines.headline: On HotPotQA, a multihop program compiled with ensembling reaches 54.7 dev answer exact match with GPT-3.5.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DSPy supports rapid development of effective systems with small LMs, and wider task reporting is deferred to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers advanced signatures, a comparison with LangChain and LlamaIndex, and long prompts from existing libraries and DSPy.

repos.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
repos.paper_summary:
AutoGen is an open-source framework for building LLM applications via multi-agent conversations. The system defines two core concepts: conversable agents, which are customizable entities backed by LLMs, tools, or human inputs, and conversation programming, a method that structures application logic around inter-agent message passing and control flow. Agents use unified interfaces to send messages and generate replies, with an auto-reply mechanism driving the workflow without a central controller. Developers can program interaction patterns using Python code or natural language instructions embedded in agent prompts.

The paper evaluates AutoGen across six domains. On the MATH dataset (5000 problems), the default two-agent configuration achieved 69.48% accuracy, outperforming vanilla GPT-4 at 55.18%. In ALFWorld decision-making tasks, adding a "grounding" agent improved performance by 15% over a ReAct baseline. For coding tasks on OptiGuide, a multi-agent design increased the F-1 score for identifying unsafe code by 8% with GPT-4 and 35% with GPT-3.5-turbo compared to a single-agent setup. The framework reduced the core workflow code for one application from 430 lines to 100 lines. Limitations include the reliance on proprietary models like GPT-4 for peak performance and the lack of formal safety guarantees for fully autonomous agent interactions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-agent conversation is proposed as the basis for building LLM applications, implemented in the AutoGen framework.

digest_headlines.heading: The AutoGen Framework
digest_headlines.headline: AutoGen rests on conversable agents and conversation programming, where agents exchange messages and control flow emerges from those conversations.

digest_headlines.heading: Applications of AutoGen
digest_headlines.headline: Six example applications test AutoGen across math, retrieval, decision making, coding, group chat and chess.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The discussion frames AutoGen as a general framework and states that its experiments are early, with safety questions left open.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics statement
digest_headlines.headline: The ethics statement names privacy, bias, accountability, trust and unintended consequences as risks to address.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work with a comparison table, expanded discussion, usage guidelines, future work, and supporting figures.

repos.title: DeltaBox: Scaling Stateful AI Agents with Millisecond-Level Sandbox Checkpoint/Rollback
repos.paper_summary: DeltaBox is an agent sandbox that checkpoints and rolls back filesystem and process state in milliseconds by duplicating only the changes between consecutive checkpoints. It relies on two OS mechanisms. DeltaFS extends Linux overlayfs: each checkpoint freezes the writable layer and inserts a new one, so rollback is a layer switch without unmounting. DeltaCR runs a CRIU dump and forks a frozen template process at each checkpoint. Restore forks the template on a hit and uses CRIU lazy-page restore on a miss. Both steps run during the LLM inference wait. On SWE-bench MCTS workloads, state-management overhead falls from 23–48% of total time on the E2B baseline to 1–2%. The paper reports that a checkpoint's ≈10.83 ms of local work is hidden under inference and that a template-fork restore takes ≈1.86 ms. Stated limitations: network I/O is not rolled back, so external side effects persist, and evicting a template sends restores to the slower CRIU path, whose latency the text does not quantify. The claimed reduction "by orders of magnitude" over baselines has no supporting baseline numbers in the text provided.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Full-state duplication makes sandbox checkpoints cost hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, too slow for frequent agent rollback.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Existing sandboxes either lack process-state rollback or snapshot whole virtual machines, so none covers both state dimensions efficiently.

digest_headlines.heading: System Overview
digest_headlines.headline: Each checkpoint stores only its per-step change, and rollback switches overlay layers then forks a warm template or restores a dump.

digest_headlines.heading: Detailed Design
digest_headlines.headline: The design swaps overlay layers at runtime and forks frozen templates, with a proxy keeping network sockets out of forked processes.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: The prototype adds about 565 lines of C to overlayfs and about 1200 lines of Python for the userspace daemon.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On SWE-bench tree-search trajectories, DeltaBox restores in 1.86 ms on weighted average, versus 899.7 ms for the incremental-snapshot baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior agent sandboxes offer coarse rollback, and serverless restore work targets cold starts rather than repeated rollback within one task.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Change-based checkpointing through DeltaFS and DeltaCR gives agent sandboxes millisecond-level rollback for search and reinforcement learning.

repos.title: GroundingPI: A Grounding Foundation Model towards Physical Intelligence with Visual Primitives
repos.paper_summary:
GroundingPI is a 4B-parameter grounding foundation model that outputs points and boxes as quantized coordinate tokens in a shared vocabulary. It is trained with multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO reinforcement learning. On 34 grounding benchmarks spanning 11 perceptual capabilities, it averages 73.68% against 44 baselines, above GPT-6 Astra at 71.54%. Metrics are F1 with mIoU for boxes and OCR, F1 at point for pointing, and task accuracy otherwise. As a visual backbone in a shared flow-matching action head, it outperforms every evaluated mainstream backbone in four out-of-distribution RoboTwin 2.0 settings, by up to 24.8% relative to the strongest. On RoboCasa-GR1 it reaches baseline-level results with 50% of demonstrations versus 75% for the baselines. On nuScenes trajectory prediction it reaches an open-loop L2 error of 0.296 m. Driving uses a language-token trajectory interface with cross-entropy training.

The paper reports gaps on tiny-box localization, high-IoU boundaries, TotalText OCR, FSC147 visual prompting, and GUI grounding. Baseline prompt and parser incompatibilities limit several comparisons, and the manipulation pretrained backbones differ in scale and supervision. Driving is evaluated open loop only.

digest_headlines.heading: Abstract
digest_headlines.headline: The abstract presents GroundingPI, a grounding foundation model meant to improve perception for robot manipulation and driving.

digest_headlines.heading: Contents
digest_headlines.headline: The contents list is empty, so the supplied text's section order is the only structure available.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix Contents
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix contents list is empty in the supplied text.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Precise grounding is needed for physical intelligence, yet general-purpose backbones still fail on dense scenes and tiny objects.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior grounding models and policy recipes add perception as task-specific proxies rather than a native foundation capability.

digest_headlines.heading: GroundingPI: A Grounding Foundation Model
digest_headlines.headline: GroundingPI outputs boxes and points as quantized coordinates in one shared vocabulary, trained by fine-tuning and GRPO.

digest_headlines.heading: GroundingPI Model towards Physical Intelligence
digest_headlines.headline: Transfer setup fixes the action learner and swaps only the perceptual backbone for driving and manipulation.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: GroundingPI averages 73.68% across 34 benchmarks, above GPT-6 Astra's 71.54%, but trails Astra on some tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Conclusion argues that precise perception suits fast execution while broad reasoning models handle planning.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers the protocol, architecture, data engine, training stages, and qualitative grounding examples.

repos.title: Skill Training with Corruption and Reconstruction Loop
repos.paper_summary: Skill Training with Corruption and Reconstruction Loop proposes a self-supervised way for LLM agents to learn domain skills as an external text library, without updating model weights, human annotations, or external rewards. Human-written short-drama screenplays are corrupted into story outlines, and the agent reconstructs each script using its skill library. A loss agent compares the reconstruction with the original and produces a textual loss report, and a backward agent edits the relevant skill cards. Skill cards are routed into Mixture-of-Experts folders, and a linter caps each card at 1,200 tokens to limit memorization. Training uses 20 novels with three epochs and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Evaluation holds out six novels (385 episodes) and compares four configurations: Base (empty library), +Few-shot, +Distill, and +Ours. The paper reports ten event-based metrics designed with professionals, and the abstract states that generation quality improves on unseen stories. The main limitations are that the training corpus is proprietary and that the evaluation is limited to short-drama screenwriting.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning large language models is costly and opaque, and hand-written skills are a bottleneck, motivating self-supervised skill acquisition.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior skill methods need costly human writing or successful trajectories, so the authors summarize and reconstruct high-quality examples instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A corruption-and-reconstruction loop trains a skill library, with capacity limits and micro-step updates to keep it organized.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Held-out evaluation compares four configurations across 385 episodes from six unseen stories using ten metrics.

repos.title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
repos.paper_summary: OmniEdu is an open family of K–12 educational foundation models (4B, 9B, and 27B, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 bases) trained on a corpus organized around four capabilities: subject competence, curriculum grounding, diagnostic reasoning, and pedagogical action and scaffolding. A six-stage pipeline cleans and decontaminates sources, audits and rewrites examples with an LLM, scores quality on 1–5 rubrics, and performs token-budgeted diversity selection with k-center greedy over BGE-M3 embeddings. Each example then receives one of 20 task-specific pedagogical system instructions. The final mixture has 69,999 examples (60,951 education-specific) and 15.96M supervised response tokens. Models are trained with LlamaFactory for 3 epochs and compared with base models, open educational LLMs, and proprietary models. OmniEdu-27B reaches 63.12% EM and 76.69% F1 on K12-Bench (base 52.11% EM), 85.89% on MathFish, 86.95% MaC on EDUMATH, 78.74% Scaffold win rate on MathTutorBench, and a 3.02 Teaching average on LongTutor. Limitations: the paper reports that EDUMATH MaC trails Kimi-K3 (90.00%), and the pipeline depends on proprietary LLM auditors and scorers.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Educational models need problem solving, curriculum structure, diagnosis, and teaching, but these are often built and tested separately.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans open educational models, data-selection methods, and benchmarks, while many frontier tutoring systems remain closed.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Preparation
digest_headlines.headline: A six-stage pipeline cleans, audits, scores, and selects 60,951 education examples, then adds general data and pedagogical instructions for 69,999 examples.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Tuning improves each base model at all three scales across curriculum, problem-solving, and tutoring benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues capability-balanced supervision yields educational models that go beyond problem solving.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists per-subtask curriculum and general-capability tables and the full training configuration.

repos.title: OpenVoice: Versatile Instant Voice Cloning
repos.paper_summary: OpenVoice is an instant voice cloning system that copies a speaker's tone color from a short reference clip while separately controlling emotion, accent, rhythm, pauses, intonation, and language. It splits the task into a base speaker TTS model (a modified VITS that takes style and language embeddings) and a feed-forward tone color converter. The converter uses an encoder, an invertible normalizing flow conditioned on a tone color vector, and HiFi-GAN decoding. The flow is trained with a KL loss against IPA phoneme features, which removes tone color from the content representation; the reference tone color is then inserted by running the flow in reverse. The base model was trained on about 30K sentences from four speakers, and the converter on 300K samples from 20K speakers. The paper reports no quantitative comparison against baselines; evaluation is qualitative, with audio on a demo site. Speed is 12× real-time on one A10G GPU (85 ms per second of speech). Cross-lingual cloning to unseen languages works when a base speaker exists for the target language. Limitations: emotion can be slightly neutralized in some cases, and the estimated 40× real-time upper bound is not yet reached.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Instant voice cloning needs a short reference clip, but existing methods lack style control and multi-language cloning without large multi-speaker data.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVoice decouples a base speaker text-to-speech model for style and language from a tone color converter that adds the reference voice.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVoice is evaluated qualitatively rather than against baselines, reaching 12 times real-time speed on one graphics processing unit.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Decoupling tone color from style and language is presented as the core principle, with code and weights released.

repos.title: KVMem: Virtualizing Million-Token Agent Workspaces on a Consumer GPU
repos.paper_summary:
KVMem is a KV-context virtualization system that preserves overflowed agent workspace history as paged KV state across GPU memory, host memory, and NVMe. Instead of compacting older context into lossy text summaries or retrieving it as text for repeated prefill, KVMem materializes a query-dependent execution view bounded by the model’s native context window. It uses step-level memory scheduling to update the historical working set once per agent step, query-conditioned retrieval via compact Mean-K indexes derived from the serving model’s attention space, and tiered KV management with position-consistent re-RoPE to restore selected blocks efficiently.

On LongMemEval-S, MemoryAgentBench, and AgentLongBench, KVMem generally achieves higher task utility than compaction-based approaches and reduces post-compaction recovery latency by 11.4–53.8× compared to Compact+RAG. In a DeepSWE long-context test with Qwen3.8-27B, KVMem improves task success from 43.8% to 48.4%. On a consumer laptop with a 24 GB RTX 5090 Laptop GPU, KVMem supports a 1M-token virtual workspace—four times the model’s 256K-token context window—while sustaining approximately 50 tokens/s in single-session generation. Limitations include the fact that reused KV state is not mathematically equivalent to recomputing text under new contexts, and that retrieval may miss task-relevant blocks if the active execution view is too small.

repos.title: LMCache: An Efficient KV Cache Layer for Enterprise-Scale LLM Inference
repos.paper_summary: LMCache is an open-source library that extracts, stores, and transfers KV caches for LLM inference engines like vLLM and SGLang. It supports cross-query prefix caching and prefill-decode disaggregation by moving data between GPU memory, CPU DRAM, local disks, and remote storage. The system optimizes data movement using batched operations with configurable chunk sizes, layer-wise pipelining to overlap compute and I/O, and zero-copy mechanisms to minimize data duplication. A modular connector interface decouples LMCache from the evolving APIs of inference engines. In evaluations on H100 GPUs across six models, LMCache achieves up to 15× higher throughput and 2× lower latency compared to basic vLLM and commercial baselines. For prefill-decode disaggregation, it reduces mean time-to-first-token by 1.53–1.84× relative to native vLLM implementation. Limitations include reduced effectiveness at low network bandwidths; loading from remote storage only outperforms full prefill when input contexts exceed 256K tokens at 32 Gbps bandwidth. Additionally, context truncation in production environments can reduce prefix cache hit rates by half.
